did_you_know.text: Did you know? The repeated wording “you shall surely return it” emphasizes that one must make a real effort to return the lost animal.
Did you know? The Hebrew word for “lost property” comes from the root meaning “to be lost”; it refers to something that has a rightful owner.
Did you know? The Torah does not merely require telling the owner about the fallen animal; it commands helping him lift it up.
Did you know? The command of sending away the mother bird teaches that even when a person takes the eggs or chicks, the mother must not be taken with them.
Did you know? The promise of “well-being and long life” also appears with honoring parents, so the Sages viewed these as two examples of identical reward language in the Torah.
Did you know? A ma’akeh is a safety barrier around a roof or other high place. Many homes in the ancient world had flat roofs, so falling from one was a real danger.
Did you know? The word kilayim refers to a mixture of different kinds forbidden by the Torah; here the example is planting different crops in one vineyard.
Did you know? An ox and a donkey differ greatly in size and strength, so making them plow together could burden both and harm the weaker animal.
Did you know? Sha’atnez is the biblical term for a mixture of wool and linen. The word is rare in the Bible and appears only in contexts concerning forbidden clothing.
Did you know? The commandment of tzitzit is connected here with a four-cornered garment. Jewish tradition later developed the tallit katan and tallit, each with four corners bearing tzitzit.
